title: ICON: Intent-Context Coupling for Efficient Multi-Turn Jailbreak Attack
summary: Multi-turn jailbreak attacks have emerged as a critical threat to Large Language Models (LLMs), bypassing safety mechanisms by progressively constructing adversarial contexts from scratch and incrementally refining prompts. However, existing methods suffer from the inefficiency of incremental context construction that requires step-by-step LLM interaction, and often stagnate in suboptimal regions due to surface-level optimization. In this paper, we characterize the Intent-Context Coupling phenomenon, revealing that LLM safety constraints are significantly relaxed when a malicious intent is coupled with a semantically congruent context pattern. Driven by this insight, we propose ICON, an automated multi-turn jailbreak framework that efficiently constructs an authoritative-style context via prior-guided semantic routing. Specifically, ICON first routes the malicious intent to a congruent context pattern (e.g., Scientific Research) and instantiates it into an attack prompt sequence. This sequence progressively builds the authoritative-style context and ultimately elicits prohibited content. In addition, ICON incorporates a Hierarchical Optimization Strategy that combines local prompt refinement with global context switching, preventing the attack from stagnating in ineffective contexts. Experimental results across eight SOTA LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of ICON, achieving a state-of-the-art average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 97.1\%. Code is available at https://github.com/xwlin-roy/ICON.

AI.tldr: ICON is an automated multi-turn jailbreak framework that exploits Intent-Context Coupling in LLMs, using semantic routing and hierarchical optimization to build authoritative contexts and achieve a 97.1% attack success rate across major LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-turn jailbreak methods are inefficient due to step-by-step context construction and often get trapped in suboptimal contexts due to shallow optimization. The authors aim to improve attack efficiency and effectiveness by exploiting deeper semantic alignments between intent and context.
AI.method: ICON employs prior-guided semantic routing to map malicious intents to semantically congruent context patterns (e.g., Scientific Research), generating an authoritative-style context through a sequence of prompts. It uses a Hierarchical Optimization Strategy combining local refinement and global context switching to avoid stagnation and enhance attack efficacy.
AI.result: ICON achieves a state-of-the-art average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 97.1% across eight state-of-the-art LLMs, outperforming existing jailbreak techniques in both effectiveness and robustness.
AI.conclusion: ICON represents a significant advancement in multi-turn jailbreak attacks on LLMs by leveraging the Intent-Context Coupling phenomenon and hierarchical optimization to achieve high attack success rates, indicating a critical vulnerability in current LLM safety mechanisms.

title: Operationalizing Research Software for Supply Chain Security
summary:
Empirical studies of research software are hard to compare because the literature operationalizes ``research software'' inconsistently. Motivated by the research software supply chain (RSSC) and its security risks, we introduce an RSSC-oriented taxonomy that makes scope and operational boundaries explicit for empirical research software security studies.
  We conduct a targeted scoping review of recent repository mining and dataset construction studies, extracting each work's definition, inclusion criteria, unit of analysis, and identification heuristics. We synthesize these into a harmonized taxonomy and a mapping that translates prior approaches into shared taxonomy dimensions. We operationalize the taxonomy on a large community-curated corpus from the Research Software Encyclopedia (RSE), producing an annotated dataset, a labeling codebook, and a reproducible labeling pipeline. Finally, we apply OpenSSF Scorecard as a preliminary security analysis to show how repository-centric security signals differ across taxonomy-defined clusters and why taxonomy-aware stratification is necessary for interpreting RSSC security measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an RSSC-oriented taxonomy to standardize the definition and operational boundaries of research software in empirical security studies, supported by a scoping review, harmonized classification, and application to a real-world dataset using OpenSSF Scorecard.
AI.motivation: Existing studies on research software lack consistency in defining and operationalizing 'research software,' especially in the context of research software supply chain (RSSC) security, making comparisons difficult. The authors aim to address this by introducing a clear, standardized taxonomy.
AI.method: The authors conduct a targeted scoping review of recent repository mining and dataset construction studies, extracting definitions, inclusion criteria, units of analysis, and identification heuristics. They synthesize these into a harmonized taxonomy and apply it to a large, community-curated corpus from the Research Software Encyclopedia (RSE), creating an annotated dataset, a labeling codebook, and a reproducible pipeline. They then apply OpenSSF Scorecard for preliminary security analysis across taxonomy-defined clusters.
AI.result: The work results in a structured, RSSC-oriented taxonomy with clear operational boundaries, a mapping of prior studies into this taxonomy, an annotated dataset from RSE, and a reproducible labeling pipeline. Preliminary security analysis using OpenSSF Scorecard shows significant differences in security signals across taxonomy-defined clusters, demonstrating the importance of taxonomy-aware stratification.
AI.conclusion: A standardized, RSSC-oriented taxonomy is essential for enabling comparable, reproducible, and meaningful empirical research on research software security. The proposed framework improves clarity, facilitates cross-study comparisons, and supports more accurate interpretation of security metrics in the research software ecosystem.

title: Robust Federated Learning for Malicious Clients using Loss Trend Deviation Detection
summary: Federated Learning (FL) facilitates collaborative model training among distributed clients while ensuring that raw data remains on local devices.Despite this advantage, FL systems are still exposed to risks from malicious or unreliable participants. Such clients can interfere with the training process by sending misleading updates, which can negatively affect the performance and reliability of the global model. Many existing defense mechanisms rely on gradient inspection, complex similarity computations, or cryptographic operations, which introduce additional overhead and may become unstable under non-IID data distributions. In this paper, we propose the Federated Learning with Loss Trend Detection (FL-LTD), a lightweight and privacy-preserving defense framework that detects and mitigates malicious behavior by monitoring temporal loss dynamics rather than model gradients. The proposed approach identifies anomalous clients by detecting abnormal loss stagnation or abrupt loss fluctuations across communication rounds. To counter adaptive attackers, a short-term memory mechanism is incorporated to sustain mitigation for clients previously flagged as anomalous, while enabling trust recovery for stable participants. We evaluate FL-LTD on a non-IID federated MNIST setup under loss manipulation attacks. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly enhances robustness, achieving a final test accuracy of 0.84, compared to 0.41 for standard FedAvg under attack. FL-LTD incurs negligible computational and communication overhead, maintains stable convergence, and avoids client exclusion or access to sensitive data, highlighting the effectiveness of loss-based monitoring for secure federated learning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FL-LTD, a lightweight and privacy-preserving defense for federated learning that detects malicious clients by monitoring temporal loss trends instead of gradients. It effectively mitigates attacks under non-IID settings with minimal overhead and no data exposure.
AI.motivation: Despite preserving data privacy, federated learning remains vulnerable to malicious participants who send misleading model updates. Existing defenses often rely on gradient analysis, similarity computations, or cryptography, which introduce computational overhead and instability, especially under non-IID data; thus, a lightweight, privacy-preserving, and robust alternative is needed.
AI.method: The paper proposes Federated Learning with Loss Trend Detection (FL-LTD), a defense mechanism that monitors temporal loss dynamics across communication rounds to detect anomalous clients. It identifies abnormal loss stagnation or abrupt fluctuations and incorporates a short-term memory mechanism to sustain mitigation for previously flagged clients while allowing trust recovery for benign ones.
AI.result: Evaluated on a non-IID federated MNIST setup under loss manipulation attacks, FL-LTD achieves a final test accuracy of 0.84, significantly outperforming standard FedAvg, which drops to 0.41. The method incurs negligible computational and communication overhead, maintains stable convergence, and avoids client exclusion or access to raw data.
AI.conclusion: FL-LTD effectively enhances the robustness of federated learning against malicious clients by leveraging loss trend monitoring without accessing sensitive data or incurring significant overhead, demonstrating that loss-based anomaly detection is a practical and effective strategy for secure FL.

title: Towards Comprehensive Benchmarking Infrastructure for LLMs In Software Engineering
comment: Short paper from bechmarking for software engineering workshop FSE2025
summary: Large language models for code are advancing fast, yet our ability to evaluate them lags behind. Current benchmarks focus on narrow tasks and single metrics, which hide critical gaps in robustness, interpretability, fairness, efficiency, and real-world usability. They also suffer from inconsistent data engineering practices, limited software engineering context, and widespread contamination issues. To understand these problems and chart a path forward, we combined an in-depth survey of existing benchmarks with insights gathered from a dedicated community workshop. We identified three core barriers to reliable evaluation: the absence of software-engineering-rich datasets, overreliance on ML-centric metrics, and the lack of standardized, reproducible data pipelines. Building on these findings, we introduce BEHELM, a holistic benchmarking infrastructure that unifies software-scenario specification with multi-metric evaluation. BEHELM provides a structured way to assess models across tasks, languages, input and output granularities, and key quality dimensions. Our goal is to reduce the overhead currently required to construct benchmarks while enabling a fair, realistic, and future-proof assessment of LLMs in software engineering.

AI.tldr: Existing code LLM benchmarks are inadequate due to narrow focus and methodological flaws. This paper presents BEHELM, a holistic benchmarking framework that enables realistic, standardized, and multi-faceted evaluation of code LLMs in software engineering contexts.
AI.motivation: Current code LLM benchmarks are narrow, inconsistent, and lack real-world software engineering context, leading to unreliable evaluations. Issues such as metric overreliance, data contamination, and missing robustness and fairness assessments hinder progress. There is a pressing need for more comprehensive, standardized, and reproducible evaluation frameworks.
AI.method: The authors conducted a comprehensive survey of existing benchmarks and gathered insights from a dedicated community workshop to identify key limitations in current evaluation practices. Based on the findings, they designed BEHELM, a benchmarking framework that integrates software-scenario specification with multi-metric evaluation across multiple dimensions.
AI.result: The study identifies three core barriers: absence of software-engineering-rich datasets, overreliance on ML-centric metrics, and lack of standardized data pipelines. BEHELM is introduced as a solution that supports multi-dimensional evaluation across tasks, programming languages, granularity levels, and quality dimensions like robustness, fairness, and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: BEHELM offers a holistic and structured benchmarking infrastructure for evaluating code LLMs more reliably and realistically by addressing core challenges in current evaluation practices, enabling fair and future-proof assessment in software engineering contexts.

title: FIPS 204-Compatible Threshold ML-DSA via Masked Lagrange Reconstruction
comment: 50 pages, 10 tables
summary:
We present masked Lagrange reconstruction, a technique that enables threshold ML-DSA (FIPS 204) with arbitrary thresholds $T$ while producing standard 3.3 KB signatures verifiable by unmodified FIPS 204 implementations. Concurrent approaches have limitations: Bienstock et al. (ePrint 2025/1163) achieve arbitrary $T$ but require honest-majority and 37--136 rounds; Celi et al. (ePrint 2026/013) achieve dishonest-majority but are limited to $T \leq 6$. Our technique addresses the barrier that Lagrange coefficients grow as $Θ(q)$ for moderate $T$, making individual contributions too large for ML-DSA's rejection sampling.
  Unlike ECDSA threshold schemes where pairwise masks suffice for correctness, ML-DSA requires solving three additional challenges absent in prior work: (1) rejection sampling on $\|z\|_\infty$ must still pass after masking, (2) the $r_0$-check exposes $c s_2$ enabling key recovery if unprotected, and (3) the resulting Irwin-Hall nonce distribution must preserve EUF-CMA security. We solve all three.
  We instantiate this technique in three deployment profiles with full security proofs. Profile P1 (TEE-assisted) achieves 3-round signing with a trusted coordinator, with EUF-CMA security under Module-SIS. Profile P2 (fully distributed) eliminates hardware trust via MPC in 8 rounds, achieving UC security against malicious adversaries corrupting up to $n-1$ parties. Profile P3 (2PC-assisted) uses lightweight 2PC for the $r_0$-check in 3--5 rounds, achieving UC security under a 1-of-2 CP honest assumption with the best empirical performance (249ms).
  Our scheme requires $|S| \geq T+1$ signers and achieves success rates of 23--32\%, matching single-signer ML-DSA.

AI.tldr: This paper presents masked Lagrange reconstruction for threshold ML-DSA (FIPS 204), enabling arbitrary thresholds with standard signature output, addressing key challenges in rejection sampling and leakage, and offering three secure deployment profiles with practical performance.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from limitations in existing threshold ML-DSA schemes: either requiring honest-majority and many rounds, or being restricted to small thresholds. The goal is to enable arbitrary thresholds with standard signature compatibility and strong security under realistic adversarial models.
AI.method: The authors introduce masked Lagrange reconstruction to address the challenges of threshold ML-DSA, specifically handling rejection sampling, the $r_0$-check leakage, and nonce distribution security. They propose three deployment profiles: TEE-assisted, fully distributed MPC, and 2PC-assisted, each with rigorous security proofs.
AI.result: The proposed scheme supports arbitrary threshold $T$, produces standard 3.3 KB signatures, and operates in 3–8 rounds depending on the profile. It achieves 23–32% success rates, matching single-signer ML-DSA, with Profile P3 showing the best performance at 249ms. Security is proven in EUF-CMA and UC models under standard assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that masked Lagrange reconstruction is a viable and efficient method for achieving threshold ML-DSA with arbitrary thresholds, compatible with standard FIPS 204 verification, and secure across multiple deployment models.

title: The Quiet Contributions: Insights into AI-Generated Silent Pull Requests
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, accepted at MSR Mining Challenge 2026
summary: We present the first empirical study of AI-generated pull requests that are 'silent,' meaning no comments or discussions accompany them. This absence of any comments or discussions associated with such silent AI pull requests (SPRs) poses a unique challenge in understanding the rationale for their acceptance or rejection. Hence, we quantitatively study 4,762 SPRs of five AI agents made to popular Python repositories drawn from the AIDev public dataset. We examine SPRs impact on code complexity, other quality issues, and security vulnerabilities, especially to determine whether these insights can hint at the rationale for acceptance or rejection of SPRs.

AI.tldr: First empirical study on silent AI-generated pull requests (SPRs) without comments, analyzing 4,762 SPRs from five AI agents in popular Python repositories to understand acceptance/rejection rationales.
AI.motivation: The lack of discussion in silent AI pull requests makes it difficult to understand why they are accepted or rejected; this study aims to uncover underlying factors such as code quality and security.
AI.method: Quantitative analysis of 4,762 silent AI pull requests from the AIDev dataset across popular Python repositories, evaluating impact on code complexity, quality issues, and security vulnerabilities.
AI.result: The study identifies patterns in how SPRs affect code quality and security, providing empirical insights that may explain their acceptance or rejection despite the absence of discussions.
AI.conclusion: Analyzing code metrics of silent AI pull requests can reveal implicit criteria for their evaluation, offering guidance for improving AI-assisted software development practices.

title: What Are Brands Telling You About Smishing? A Cross-Industry Evaluation of Customer Guidance
summary: Phishing attacks through text, also known as smishing, are a prevalent type of social engineering tactic in which attackers impersonate brands to deceive victims into providing personal information and/or money. While smishing awareness and cyber education are a key method by which organizations communicate this awareness, the guidance itself varies widely. In this paper, we investigate the state of practice of how 149 well-known brands across 25 categories educate their customers about smishing and what smishing prevention and reporting advice they provide. After conducting a comprehensive content analysis of the brands, we identified significant gaps in the smishing-related information provided: only 46\% of the 149 brands mentioned the definition of smishing, less than 1\% had a video tutorial on smishing, and only 50\% of brands provided instructions on how to report. Our study highlights variation in terminology, prevention advice, and reporting mechanisms across industries, with some brands recommending potentially ineffective strategies such as "ignoring suspicious messages." These findings establish a baseline for understanding the current state of industry smishing awareness advice and provide specific areas where standardization improvements are needed. From our evaluation, we provide recommendations for brands on how to offer streamlined education to their respective customers on smishing for better awareness and protection against increasing smishing attacks.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes smishing education practices across 149 brands, revealing major gaps in awareness content, inconsistent advice, and poor reporting guidance, calling for standardized customer education.
AI.motivation: To understand the current state of practice in how brands educate customers about smishing and to identify gaps and inconsistencies in guidance.
AI.method: Conducted a comprehensive content analysis of 149 well-known brands across 25 categories to evaluate their smishing education, prevention advice, and reporting instructions.
AI.result: Only 46% of brands defined smishing, less than 1% provided video tutorials, and 50% offered reporting instructions. Advice varies widely, with some recommending ineffective measures like ignoring suspicious messages.
AI.conclusion: There is a significant lack of standardized and comprehensive smishing awareness education provided by brands, indicating a need for improved, consistent, and effective customer education and reporting mechanisms.

title: Adaptive and Robust Cost-Aware Proof of Quality for Decentralized LLM Inference Networks
summary:
Decentralized large language model inference networks require lightweight mechanisms to reward high quality outputs under heterogeneous latency and cost. Proof of Quality provides scalable verification by sampling evaluator nodes that score candidate outputs, then aggregating their scores into a consensus signal that determines rewards. However, evaluator heterogeneity and malicious score manipulation can distort consensus and inflate payouts, which weakens incentive alignment in open participation settings.
  This paper extends a cost-aware Proof of Quality mechanism by adding adversary-resilient consensus formation. We study robust aggregation rules, including median and trimmed mean, and an adaptive trust-weighted consensus that updates evaluator weights from deviation signals. Using question answering and summarization workloads with a ground truth proxy for offline analysis, we quantify evaluator reliability and show strong variance across evaluators, including task-dependent misalignment that can invert correlations. We then evaluate robustness under four adversarial strategies, including noise injection, boosting, sabotage, and intermittent manipulation, across a sweep of malicious ratios and evaluator sample sizes. Our results show that robust aggregation improves consensus alignment with the ground truth proxy and reduces sensitivity to noisy and strategic attacks compared with simple averaging. We further characterize the operational trade-off introduced by evaluator sampling, where larger evaluator sets reduce evaluator rewards and increase payoff variance while inference rewards remain relatively stable in our configuration. These findings motivate robust consensus as a default component for cost-aware Proof of Quality and provide practical guidance for selecting evaluator sampling parameters under adversarial risk and resource constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper enhances cost-aware Proof of Quality in decentralized LLM inference by introducing adversary-resilient consensus mechanisms, showing that robust aggregation rules (e.g., median, trimmed mean, trust-weighted) improve alignment with ground truth and reduce vulnerability to adversarial manipulation under varied attack strategies.
AI.motivation: In decentralized LLM inference networks, fair reward distribution depends on accurate output evaluation. However, evaluator heterogeneity and malicious behavior can distort consensus in Proof of Quality systems, weakening incentives. The need for robust, scalable, and cost-aware evaluation motivates resilient consensus formation.
AI.method: The authors extend a cost-aware Proof of Quality framework with robust consensus aggregation methods—median, trimmed mean, and adaptive trust-weighted consensus that adjusts evaluator weights based on deviation from group scores. They conduct offline experiments using question answering and summarization tasks with a ground truth proxy, evaluating performance under four adversarial strategies (noise injection, boosting, sabotage, intermittent manipulation) across varying malicious ratios and evaluator sample sizes.
AI.result: Significant evaluator variance and task-dependent misalignment are observed, sometimes inverting score correlations. Robust aggregation methods outperform simple averaging by improving consensus alignment with the ground truth proxy and reducing sensitivity to attacks. Larger evaluator sets decrease individual rewards and increase payoff variance, while inference rewards remain stable.
AI.conclusion: Robust consensus aggregation is essential for securing incentive alignment in open, decentralized LLM inference networks. The study advocates for adopting robust rules as default in Proof of Quality systems and provides actionable guidance on evaluator sampling under adversarial and resource-constrained conditions.

title: From Logic to Toolchains: An Empirical Study of Bugs in the TypeScript Ecosystem
summary: TypeScript has rapidly become a popular language for modern web development, yet its effect on software faults remains poorly understood. This paper presents the first large-scale empirical study of bugs in real-world TypeScript projects. We analyze 633 bug reports from 16 popular open-source repositories to construct a taxonomy of fault types, quantify their prevalence, and relate them to project characteristics such as size, domain, and dependency composition. Our results reveal a fault landscape dominated not by logic or syntax errors but by tooling and configuration faults, API misuses, and asynchronous error-handling issues. We show that these categories correlate strongly with build complexity and dependency heterogeneity, indicating that modern failures often arise at integration and orchestration boundaries rather than within algorithmic logic. A longitudinal comparison with JavaScript studies shows that while static typing in TypeScript has reduced traditional runtime and type errors, it has shifted fragility toward build systems and toolchains. These findings offer new insight into how language design and ecosystem evolution reshape the fault profiles of large-scale software systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first large-scale empirical study on bugs in real-world TypeScript projects, analyzing 633 bug reports from 16 open-source repositories. It reveals that the majority of faults are not traditional logic or syntax errors but stem from tooling/configuration issues, API misuses, and asynchronous error handling, which are closely tied to build complexity and dependency diversity. The study shows that while TypeScript’s static typing reduces runtime and type errors, it shifts software fragility to build systems and toolchains.
AI.motivation: Despite TypeScript's growing popularity in modern web development, little is known about its actual impact on software reliability and fault characteristics. Understanding how TypeScript influences the types and distribution of bugs is crucial for improving language design, tooling, and development practices.
AI.method: The authors conducted a large-scale empirical analysis of 633 bug reports from 16 popular open-source TypeScript repositories. They constructed a taxonomy of fault types through qualitative and quantitative analysis, and examined correlations between fault categories and project attributes such as size, domain, and dependency composition. They also performed a longitudinal comparison with prior studies on JavaScript to assess the impact of TypeScript’s static typing.
AI.result: The study found that the most prevalent faults in TypeScript are tooling and configuration issues, API misuses, and asynchronous error-handling problems—not logic or syntax errors. These fault types strongly correlate with build complexity and dependency heterogeneity. Compared to JavaScript, TypeScript reduces traditional runtime and type errors but introduces new fragilities in build systems and development toolchains.
AI.conclusion: The adoption of TypeScript changes the nature of software faults by mitigating type-related bugs but shifting failure modes toward integration, tooling, and configuration challenges. This highlights the need for improved tooling, better ecosystem coherence, and developer support in managing build and dependency complexity in modern software development.

title: SPOILER-GUARD: Gating Latency Effects of Memory Accesses through Randomized Dependency Prediction
comment: 3 pages, 3 figures, to appear in DATE 2026 Conference Proceedings
summary: Modern microprocessors depend on speculative execution, creating vulnerabilities that enable transient execution attacks. Prior defenses target speculative data leakage but overlook false dependencies from partial address aliasing, where repeated squash and reissue events increase the load-store latency, which is exploited by the SPOILER attack. We present SPOILER-GUARD, a hardware defense that obfuscates speculative dependency resolution by dynamically randomizing the physical address bits used for load-store comparisons and tagging store entries to prevent latency-amplifying misspeculations. Implemented in gem5 and evaluated with SPEC 2017, SPOILER-GUARD reduces misspeculation to 0.0004 percent and improves integer and floating-point performance by 2.12 and 2.87 percent. HDL synthesis with Synopsys Design Compiler at 14 nm node demonstrates minimal overheads - 69 ps latency in critical path, 0.064 square millimeter in area, and 5.863 mW in power.

AI.tldr: SPOILER-GUARD is a lightweight hardware defense that prevents SPOILER attacks by randomizing physical address bits and tagging stores to eliminate false dependencies during speculative execution, achieving near-zero misspeculation with minimal performance and area cost.
AI.motivation: Existing speculative execution defenses fail to address false dependencies caused by partial address aliasing, which induce repeat squash-and-reissue events that amplify load-store latency and are exploitable via the SPOILER attack.
AI.method: SPOILER-GUARD introduces dynamic randomization of physical address bits for load-store dependency checks and uses store tagging in the memory dependence prediction logic to prevent false dependencies arising from partial address aliasing during speculative execution.
AI.result: Implementation in gem5 with SPEC 2017 benchmarks shows a reduction in misspeculation rate to 0.0004%, along with 2.12% and 2.87% improvements in integer and floating-point performance. Synthesis at 14 nm reports 69 ps latency, 0.064 mm area, and 5.863 mW power overhead.
AI.conclusion: SPOILER-GUARD effectively mitigates SPOILER-style transient execution attacks by eliminating exploitable load-store latency variations through secure speculative dependency resolution, with negligible hardware overhead and slight performance improvements.

title: Human-Agent versus Human Pull Requests: A Testing-Focused Characterization and Comparison
summary: AI-based coding agents are increasingly integrated into software development workflows, collaborating with developers to create pull requests (PRs). Despite their growing adoption, the role of human-agent collaboration in software testing remains poorly understood. This paper presents an empirical study of 6,582 human-agent PRs (HAPRs) and 3,122 human PRs (HPRs) from the AIDev dataset. We compare HAPRs and HPRs along three dimensions: (i) testing frequency and extent, (ii) types of testing-related changes (code-and-test co-evolution vs. test-focused), and (iii) testing quality, measured by test smells. Our findings reveal that, although the likelihood of including tests is comparable (42.9% for HAPRs vs. 40.0% for HPRs), HAPRs exhibit a larger extent of testing, nearly doubling the test-to-source line ratio found in HPRs. While test-focused task distributions are comparable, HAPRs are more likely to add new tests during co-evolution (OR=1.79), whereas HPRs prioritize modifying existing tests. Finally, although some test smell categories differ statistically, negligible effect sizes suggest no meaningful differences in quality. These insights provide the first characterization of how human-agent collaboration shapes testing practices.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes human-agent and human-only pull requests, finding that while testing frequency is similar, human-agent collaboration leads to greater testing extent and more new test additions during code-and-test co-evolution, with no meaningful difference in test quality as measured by test smells.
AI.motivation: Despite the growing use of AI-based coding agents in software development, little is known about how human-agent collaboration impacts software testing practices, necessitating an empirical investigation.
AI.method: The authors conducted an empirical study using 6,582 human-agent pull requests (HAPRs) and 3,122 human pull requests (HPRs) from the AIDev dataset, comparing them across testing frequency, types of testing changes (co-evolution vs. test-focused), and testing quality via test smells.
AI.result: Testing inclusion rates are similar (42.9% HAPRs vs. 40.0% HPRs), but HAPRs have nearly double the test-to-source line ratio. HAPRs are more likely to add new tests during co-evolution (OR=1.79), while HPRs favor modifying existing tests. Some test smell differences are statistically significant but have negligible effect sizes.
AI.conclusion: Human-agent collaboration increases testing extent and promotes new test creation during development, with no substantial trade-off in testing quality, offering the first empirical characterization of testing in AI-assisted development workflows.

title: Lossless Copyright Protection via Intrinsic Model Fingerprinting
summary: The exceptional performance of diffusion models establishes them as high-value intellectual property but exposes them to unauthorized replication. Existing protection methods either modify the model to embed watermarks, which impairs performance, or extract model fingerprints by manipulating the denoising process, rendering them incompatible with black-box APIs. In this paper, we propose TrajPrint, a completely lossless and training-free framework that verifies model copyright by extracting unique manifold fingerprints formed during deterministic generation. Specifically, we first utilize a watermarked image as an anchor and exactly trace the path back to its trajectory origin, effectively locking the model fingerprint mapped by this path. Subsequently, we implement a joint optimization strategy that employs dual-end anchoring to synthesize a specific fingerprint noise, which strictly adheres to the target manifold for robust watermark recovery. As input, it enables the protected target model to recover the watermarked image, while failing on non-target models. Finally, we achieved verification via atomic inference and statistical hypothesis testing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TrajPrint achieves lossless verification in black-box API scenarios with superior robustness against model modifications.

AI.tldr: TrajPrint proposes a lossless, training-free method for protecting diffusion model copyright by extracting unique manifold fingerprints during deterministic generation, enabling robust, black-box verification without degrading model performance.
AI.motivation: To protect diffusion models as intellectual property without compromising performance or requiring model modifications, especially in black-box API scenarios where existing watermarking methods fail.
AI.method: TrajPrint uses a watermarked image as an anchor to trace back the generation trajectory to its origin, locking the model's fingerprint. It employs dual-end anchoring to optimize a specific fingerprint noise that conforms to the target manifold. Verification is achieved through atomic inference and statistical hypothesis testing.
AI.result: TrajPrint enables lossless, black-box copyright verification with high robustness against model modifications. It successfully recovers watermarks only on the target model, failing on non-target models, ensuring secure and reliable ownership verification.
AI.conclusion: TrajPrint offers a novel, effective solution for diffusion model copyright protection that is completely lossless, training-free, and compatible with black-box APIs by leveraging unique manifold fingerprints from deterministic generation processes.

title: CovAgent: Overcoming the 30% Curse of Mobile Application Coverage with Agentic AI and Dynamic Instrumentation
comment: Under Review; We open-source CovAgent at https://osf.io/vxgwm/?view_only=3edf2abe5a12419fa6413933da851847
summary: Automated GUI testing is crucial for ensuring the quality and reliability of Android apps. However, the efficacy of existing UI testing techniques is often limited, especially in terms of coverage. Recent studies, including the state-of-the-art, struggle to achieve more than 30% activity coverage in real-world apps. This limited coverage can be attributed to a combination of factors such as failing to generate complex user inputs, unsatisfied activation conditions regarding device configurations and external resources, and hard-to-reach code paths that are not easily accessible through the GUI. To overcome these limitations, we propose CovAgent, a novel agentic AI-powered approach to enhance Android app UI testing. Our fuzzer-agnostic framework comprises an AI agent that inspects the app's decompiled Smali code and component transition graph, and reasons about unsatisfied activation conditions within the app code logic that prevent access to the activities that are unreachable by standard and widely adopted GUI fuzzers. Then, another agent generates dynamic instrumentation scripts that satisfy activation conditions required for successful transitions to those activities. We found that augmenting existing fuzzing approaches with our framework achieves a significant improvement in test coverage over the state-of-the-art, LLMDroid, and other baselines such as Fastbot and APE (e.g., 101.1%, 116.3% and 179.7% higher activity coverage, respectively). CovAgent also outperforms all the baselines in other metrics such as class, method, and line coverage. We also conduct investigations into components within CovAgent to reveal further insights regarding the efficacy of Agentic AI in the field of automated app testing such as the agentic activation condition inference accuracy, and agentic activity-launching success rate.

AI.tldr: CovAgent is an AI-powered, fuzzer-agnostic framework that improves Android GUI testing by analyzing Smali code and component transitions to identify and satisfy activation conditions, significantly increasing activity and code coverage over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Existing Android GUI testing tools suffer from low coverage (often <30% activity coverage) due to inability to handle complex inputs, unmet activation conditions (e.g., device state, resources), and GUI-inaccessible code paths. This limits their effectiveness in thoroughly testing real-world apps.
AI.method: CovAgent uses two AI agents: one analyzes decompiled Smali code and the component transition graph to infer activation conditions blocking access to unreachable activities; the second generates dynamic instrumentation scripts to satisfy these conditions. It is fuzzer-agnostic and integrates with existing GUI fuzzers to enable transitions to previously unreachable components.
AI.result: CovAgent significantly boosts coverage: achieves 101.1%, 116.3%, and 179.7% higher activity coverage than LLMDroid, Fastbot, and APE respectively. It also outperforms baselines in class, method, and line coverage. Ablation studies show high accuracy in activation condition inference and successful activity launching via instrumentation.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI can effectively reason about and resolve activation barriers in Android apps, substantially improving GUI testing coverage. CovAgent demonstrates that integrating AI-driven code analysis and dynamic instrumentation with existing fuzzers is a powerful approach for enhancing automated app testing.

title: Virtualization-based Penetration Testing Study for Detecting Accessibility Abuse Vulnerabilities in Banking Apps in East and Southeast Asia
comment: Accepted at APSEC 2025 Software Engineering in Practices (SEIP)
summary: Android banking applications have revolutionized financial management by allowing users to perform various financial activities through mobile devices. However, this convenience has attracted cybercriminals who exploit security vulnerabilities to access sensitive financial data. FjordPhantom, a malware identified by our industry collaborator, uses virtualization and hooking to bypass the detection of malicious accessibility services, allowing it to conduct keylogging, screen scraping, and unauthorized data access. This malware primarily affects banking and finance apps across East and Southeast Asia region where our industry partner's clients are primarily based in. It requires users to be deceived into installing a secondary malicious component and activating a malicious accessibility service. In our study, we conducted an empirical study on the susceptibility of banking apps in the region to FjordPhantom, analyzed the effectiveness of protective measures currently implemented in those apps, and discussed ways to detect and prevent such attacks by identifying and mitigating the vulnerabilities exploited by this malware.

AI.tldr: FjordPhantom is a sophisticated Android malware targeting banking apps in East and Southeast Asia using virtualization and hooking to evade detection and steal sensitive data. This study evaluates the vulnerability of regional financial apps, finds existing protections lacking, and proposes improved detection and mitigation techniques.
AI.motivation: The rise of Android banking malware like FjordPhantom threatens financial security in East and Southeast Asia, necessitating an understanding of vulnerabilities and defenses in targeted apps.
AI.method: Empirical study assessing the susceptibility of regional banking apps to FjordPhantom, analyzing existing protections, and proposing detection and prevention mechanisms.
AI.result: FjordPhantom effectively bypasses detection using virtualization and hooking, enabling keylogging, screen scraping, and unauthorized data access; many banking apps lack adequate defenses against such attacks.
AI.conclusion: Current protective measures in banking apps are insufficient against sophisticated malware like FjordPhantom, highlighting the need for enhanced detection and mitigation strategies to secure financial applications.

title: The Role of Social Identity in Shaping Biases Against Minorities in Software Organizations
summary: While systemic workplace bias is well-documented in non-computing fields, its specific impact on software engineers remains poorly understood. This study addresses that gap by applying Social Identity Theory (SIT) to investigate four distinct forms of bias: lack of career development, stereotyped task selection, unwelcoming environments, and identity attacks. Using a vignette-based survey, we quantified the prevalence of these biases, identified the demographics most affected, assessed their consequences, and explored the motivations behind biased actions. Our results show that career development and task selection biases are the most prevalent forms, with over two-thirds of victims experiencing them multiple times. Women were more than three times as likely as men to face career development bias, task selection bias, and an unwelcoming environment. In parallel, individuals from marginalized ethnic backgrounds were disproportionately targeted by identity attacks. Our analysis also confirms that, beyond gender and race, factors such as age, years of experience, organization size, and geographic location are significant predictors of bias victimization.

AI.tldr: This study applies Social Identity Theory to reveal that software engineers face significant workplace bias, especially in career development and task assignment, with women and ethnically marginalized groups disproportionately affected, and identifies multiple demographic and organizational predictors of bias.
AI.motivation: To understand the specific impact of systemic workplace bias on software engineers, which remains underexplored despite extensive documentation in non-computing fields.
AI.method: The study uses Social Identity Theory (SIT) as a framework and employs a vignette-based survey to quantify the prevalence of four forms of bias: lack of career development, stereotyped task selection, unwelcoming environments, and identity attacks. Statistical analysis identifies affected demographics and predictors of bias.
AI.result: Over two-thirds of victims experience career development and task selection biases multiple times. Women are over three times more likely than men to face career development bias, task selection bias, and unwelcoming environments. Marginalized ethnic groups are disproportionately subjected to identity attacks. Age, experience, organization size, and location are significant predictors of bias.
AI.conclusion: This paper concludes that systemic workplace bias significantly impacts software engineers, with career development and task selection biases being the most prevalent. Women and individuals from marginalized ethnic backgrounds face disproportionate levels of bias, and factors such as age, experience, organization size, and geography further predict victimization.

title: User-Centric Phishing Detection: A RAG and LLM-Based Approach
summary: The escalating sophistication of phishing emails necessitates a shift beyond traditional rule-based and conventional machine-learning-based detectors. Although large language models (LLMs) offer strong natural language understanding, using them as standalone classifiers often yields elevated falsepositive (FP) rates, which mislabel legitimate emails as phishing and create significant operational burden. This paper presents a personalized phishing detection framework that integrates LLMs with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). For each message, the system constructs user-specific context by retrieving a compact set of the user's historical legitimate emails and enriching it with real-time domain and URL reputation from a cyber-threat intelligence platform, then conditions the LLM's decision on this evidence. We evaluate four open-source LLMs (Llama4-Scout, DeepSeek-R1, Mistral-Saba, and Gemma2) on an email dataset collected from public and institutional sources. Results show high performance; for example, Llama4-Scout attains an F1-score of 0.9703 and achieves a 66.7% reduction in FPs with RAG. These findings validate that a RAG-based, user-profiling approach is both feasible and effective for building high-precision, low-friction email security systems that adapt to individual communication patterns.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a personalized phishing detection framework using LLMs enhanced with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to reduce false positives by incorporating user-specific email history and real-time threat intelligence.
AI.motivation: Traditional phishing detectors and standalone LLMs suffer from high false-positive rates, leading to operational inefficiencies; there is a need for more accurate, adaptive, and user-aware detection systems.
AI.method: The framework uses RAG to retrieve a user's historical legitimate emails and enriches this with real-time domain and URL reputation data from a cyber-threat intelligence platform, which is then used to condition the LLM's classification decision. Evaluated on four open-source LLMs (Llama4-Scout, DeepSeek-R1, Mistral-Saba, Gemma2) using a public and institutional email dataset.
AI.result: High performance is achieved, with Llama4-Scout reaching an F1-score of 0.9703 and a 66.7% reduction in false positives when RAG is applied.
AI.conclusion: The RAG-based, user-profiling approach is feasible and effective for building high-precision, low-friction phishing detection systems that adapt to individual user behavior.

title: More Code, Less Reuse: Investigating Code Quality and Reviewer Sentiment towards AI-generated Pull Requests
comment: Accepted to MSR 2026
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) Agents are advancing quickly, with the increasing leveraging of LLM Agents to assist in development tasks such as code generation. While LLM Agents accelerate code generation, studies indicate they may introduce adverse effects on development. However, existing metrics solely measure pass rates, failing to reflect impacts on long-term maintainability and readability, and failing to capture human intuitive evaluations of PR. To increase the comprehensiveness of this problem, we investigate and evaluate the characteristics of LLM to know the pull requests' characteristics beyond the pass rate. We observe the code quality and maintainability within PRs based on code metrics to evaluate objective characteristics and developers' reactions to the pull requests from both humans and LLM's generation. Evaluation results indicate that LLM Agents frequently disregard code reuse opportunities, resulting in higher levels of redundancy compared to human developers. In contrast to the quality issues, our emotions analysis reveals that reviewers tend to express more neutral or positive emotions towards AI-generated contributions than human ones. This disconnect suggests that the surface-level plausibility of AI code masks redundancy, leading to the silent accumulation of technical debt in real-world development environments. Our research provides insights for improving human-AI collaboration.

AI.tldr: LLM Agents generate functionally correct but redundant code, increasing technical debt; yet, reviewers respond more positively, indicating a disconnect between perceived and actual code quality.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation metrics for LLM-generated code focus only on functional correctness (e.g., pass rates), failing to capture long-term impacts on code maintainability, readability, and human perception. This gap motivates a deeper investigation into the broader implications of AI-generated code in software development.
AI.method: The authors analyze pull requests (PRs) generated by LLM Agents versus human developers using objective code metrics (e.g., redundancy, maintainability) and emotional sentiment analysis of reviewer feedback. They compare code quality characteristics and developer responses to assess both technical and perceptual differences.
AI.result: LLM Agents produce code with higher redundancy and lower reuse compared to human developers, indicating poorer long-term maintainability. However, sentiment analysis shows reviewers react more neutrally or positively to AI-generated PRs, suggesting that superficial code quality masks underlying technical debt.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that while LLM Agents generate code that appears plausible and elicits neutral or positive reactions from reviewers, they often introduce redundancy by disregarding code reuse, leading to silent accumulation of technical debt. This highlights a critical need for improved evaluation metrics and practices in human-AI collaborative development.

title: Towards Zero Rotation and Beyond: Architecting Neural Networks for Fast Secure Inference with Homomorphic Encryption
comment: the IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning (SaTML)
summary: Privacy-preserving deep learning addresses privacy concerns in Machine Learning as a Service (MLaaS) by using Homomorphic Encryption (HE) for linear computations. However, the computational overhead remains a major challenge. While prior work has improved efficiency, most approaches build on models originally designed for plaintext inference. Such models incur architectural inefficiencies when adapted to HE. We argue that substantial gains require networks tailored to HE rather than retrofitting plaintext architectures. Our design has two components: the building block and the overall architecture. First, StriaBlock targets the most expensive HE operation, rotation. It integrates ExRot-Free Convolution and a novel Cross Kernel, eliminating external rotations and requiring only 19% of the internal rotations used by plaintext models. Second, our architectural principles include (i) the Focused Constraint Principle, which limits cost-sensitive factors while preserving flexibility elsewhere, and (ii) the Channel Packing-Aware Scaling Principle, which adapts bottleneck ratios to ciphertext channel capacity that varies with depth. Together, these strategies control both local and end-to-end HE cost, enabling a balanced HE-tailored network. We evaluate the resulting StriaNet across datasets of varying scales, including ImageNet, Tiny ImageNet, and CIFAR-10. At comparable accuracy, StriaNet achieves speedups of 9.78x, 6.01x, and 9.24x on ImageNet, Tiny ImageNet, and CIFAR-10, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces StriaNet, a deep learning architecture specifically designed for homomorphic encryption, reducing computational overhead by eliminating external rotations and optimizing bottleneck scaling, achieving up to 9.78x faster inference with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Homomorphic encryption enables privacy-preserving deep learning but suffers from high computational overhead when using models designed for plaintext; retrofitting these models leads to inefficiencies, necessitating HE-aware architectures.
AI.method: The paper proposes StriaNet, which includes StriaBlock—a building block eliminating costly HE rotations via ExRot-Free Convolution and Cross Kernel—and two architectural principles: Focused Constraint Principle and Channel Packing-Aware Scaling Principle, both optimized for HE constraints.
AI.result: StriaNet reduces rotation operations significantly—only 19% of internal rotations used by plaintext models—and achieves speedups of 9.78x, 6.01x, and 9.24x on ImageNet, Tiny ImageNet, and CIFAR-10 respectively, with comparable accuracy.
AI.conclusion: StriaNet demonstrates that designing deep learning models specifically for homomorphic encryption, rather than adapting plaintext models, leads to significant efficiency improvements in privacy-preserving inference.

title: Detecting Multiple Semantic Concerns in Tangled Code Commits
comment: 28 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to Empirical Software Engineering (Springer)
summary: Code commits in a version control system (e.g., Git) should be atomic, i.e., focused on a single goal, such as adding a feature or fixing a bug. In practice, however, developers often bundle multiple concerns into tangled commits, obscuring intent and complicating maintenance. Recent studies have used Conventional Commits Specification (CCS) and Language Models (LMs) to capture commit intent, demonstrating that Small Language Models (SLMs) can approach the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) while maintaining efficiency and privacy. However, they do not address tangled commits involving multiple concerns, leaving the feasibility of using LMs for multi-concern detection unresolved. In this paper, we frame multi-concern detection in tangled commits as a multi-label classification problem and construct a controlled dataset of artificially tangled commits based on real-world data. We then present an empirical study using SLMs to detect multiple semantic concerns in tangled commits, examining the effects of fine-tuning, concern count, commit-message inclusion, and header-preserving truncation under practical token-budget limits. Our results show that a fine-tuned 14B-parameter SLM is competitive with a state-of-the-art LLM for single-concern commits and remains usable for up to three concerns. In particular, including commit messages improves detection accuracy by up to 44% (in terms of Hamming Loss) with negligible latency overhead, establishing them as important semantic cues.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using fine-tuned small language models for detecting multiple concerns in tangled code commits, showing that with commit message inclusion, a 14B SLM achieves LLM-level performance and significantly improves multi-concern detection accuracy.
AI.motivation: Tangled commits that bundle multiple concerns hinder code maintainability and obscure developer intent; while LMs have been used to capture commit intent, their effectiveness in identifying multiple concerns in tangled commits remains unexplored.
AI.method: The authors framed multi-concern detection in tangled commits as a multi-label classification problem, constructed a dataset of artificial tangled commits from real-world data, and conducted an empirical evaluation using SLMs under various conditions including fine-tuning, commit message inclusion, and token-limited truncation strategies.
AI.result: The fine-tuned 14B SLM performs on par with state-of-the-art LLMs for single-concern commits and maintains usability for up to three concerns. Including commit messages improves detection accuracy by up to 44% in Hamming Loss with minimal latency impact.
AI.conclusion: A fine-tuned 14B-parameter Small Language Model (SLM) is competitive with large language models in detecting multiple concerns in code commits and remains effective for up to three concerns, especially when commit messages are included.

title: SecIC3: Customizing IC3 for Hardware Security Verification
comment: Accepted by DATE 2026
summary: Recent years have seen significant advances in using formal verification to check hardware security properties. Of particular practical interest are checking confidentiality and integrity of secrets, by checking that there is no information flow between the secrets and observable outputs. A standard method for checking information flow is to translate the corresponding non-interference hyperproperty into a safety property on a self-composition of the design, which has two copies of the design composed together. Although prior efforts have aimed to reduce the size of the self-composed design, there are no state-of-the-art model checkers that exploit their special structure for hardware security verification. In this paper, we propose SecIC3, a hardware model checking algorithm based on IC3 that is customized to exploit this self-composition structure. SecIC3 utilizes this structure in two complementary techniques: symmetric state exploration and adding equivalence predicates. We implement SecIC3 on top of two open-source IC3 implementations and evaluate it on a non-interference checking benchmark consisting of 10 designs. The experiment results show that SecIC3 significantly reduces the time for finding security proofs, with up to 49.3x proof speedup compared to baseline implementations.

AI.tldr: SecIC3 is a custom hardware model checking algorithm based on IC3 that exploits the self-composition structure in non-interference verification, achieving up to 49.3x faster proof times on a benchmark of 10 designs.
AI.motivation: Formal verification of hardware security, particularly confidentiality and integrity via information flow analysis, requires efficient checking of non-interference hyperproperties. Existing model checkers do not exploit the inherent structure of self-composed designs, leading to inefficiencies in verification.
AI.method: SecIC3 is an IC3-based algorithm tailored for self-composed hardware designs used in non-interference checking. It introduces two key optimizations: symmetric state exploration, which avoids redundant state visits by leveraging structural symmetry, and equivalence predicates, which encode state equivalences between design copies to simplify the state space.
AI.result: Implemented on two open-source IC3 backends and evaluated on a 10-design benchmark, SecIC3 achieves significant proof-time reductions, with up to 49.3x speedup over baseline approaches, while maintaining correctness.
AI.conclusion: SecIC3 demonstrates that exploiting the self-composition structure in hardware security verification can dramatically improve model checking efficiency, offering a practical advancement for verifying non-interference in hardware designs.

title: Developers in the Age of AI: Adoption, Policy, and Diffusion of AI Software Engineering Tools
comment: Submitted to Empirical Software Engineering (EMSE)
summary: The rapid advance of Generative AI into software development prompts this empirical investigation of perceptual effects on practice. We study the usage patterns of 147 professional developers, examining perceived correlates of AI tools use, the resulting productivity and quality outcomes, and developer readiness for emerging AI-enhanced development. We describe a virtuous adoption cycle where frequent and broad AI tools use are the strongest correlates of both Perceived Productivity (PP) and quality, with frequency strongest. The study finds no perceptual support for the Quality Paradox and shows that PP is positively correlated with Perceived Code Quality (PQ) improvement. Developers thus report both productivity and quality gains. High current usage, breadth of application, frequent use of AI tools for testing, and ease of use correlate strongly with future intended adoption, though security concerns remain a moderate and statistically significant barrier to adoption. Moreover, AI testing tools' adoption lags that of coding tools, opening a Testing Gap. We identify three developer archetypes (Enthusiasts, Pragmatists, Cautious) that align with an innovation diffusion process wherein the virtuous adoption cycle serves as the individual engine of progression. Our findings reveal that organizational adoption of AI tools follows such a process: Enthusiasts push ahead with tools, creating organizational success that converts Pragmatists. The Cautious are held in organizational stasis: without early adopter examples, they don't enter the virtuous adoption cycle, never accumulate the usage frequency that drives intent, and never attain high efficacy. Policy itself does not predict individuals' intent to increase usage but functions as a marker of maturity, formalizing the successful diffusion of adoption by Enthusiasts while acting as a gateway that the Cautious group has yet to reach.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes the impact of Generative AI tools on professional software development across 147 developers, identifying a virtuous adoption cycle where frequent and broad use of AI tools strongly correlates with improved perceived productivity and code quality. Three developer archetypes—Enthusiasts, Pragmatists, and Cautious—are identified, aligning with innovation diffusion: early adopters drive organizational adoption, while the Cautious remain excluded without exposure. AI testing tool adoption lags behind coding tools, creating a 'Testing Gap,' and security concerns persist as a barrier. Organizational policies reflect maturity in adoption but do not directly influence individual usage intent.
AI.motivation: The rapid integration of Generative AI into software development raises questions about its real-world impact on developer practices, productivity, code quality, and organizational adoption. This study aims to empirically investigate how developers perceive and use AI tools, whether perceived gains in productivity come at the cost of quality (the so-called Quality Paradox), and how organizational and individual factors influence adoption patterns and future intent.
AI.method: The study conducts an empirical analysis of survey data from 147 professional developers, examining self-reported usage patterns, perceived productivity (PP), perceived code quality (PQ), intent to adopt, and organizational policies. Correlation and regression analyses are used to identify key predictors of PP and PQ, as well as future adoption intent. Developer archetypes are derived through cluster analysis, and their behaviors are interpreted through the lens of innovation diffusion theory.
AI.result: Frequent and broad use of AI tools is the strongest predictor of both perceived productivity and perceived code quality, with no evidence supporting the Quality Paradox. Developers report gains in both areas. Use of AI for testing, ease of use, and current usage level strongly predict future adoption intent, though security concerns remain a significant barrier. A 'Testing Gap' is observed, where AI testing tools are adopted less than coding tools. Three developer archetypes—Enthusiasts, Pragmatists, and Cautious—are identified, reflecting stages in innovation diffusion. Organizational adoption is driven by Enthusiasts, whose success converts Pragmatists, while the Cautious remain inactive without early examples. Organizational policy correlates with adoption maturity but does not predict individual usage intent.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that a virtuous adoption cycle—where increased frequency and breadth of AI tool use lead to perceived gains in productivity and quality—drives individual and organizational adoption of AI in software development. Enthusiasts serve as catalysts, enabling broader organizational diffusion. However, the Cautious remain excluded without exposure to successful use cases, highlighting a need for targeted onboarding. Security concerns and the Testing Gap represent key challenges. Organizational policies reflect but do not drive adoption, suggesting they should follow rather than precede grassroots innovation.

title: RerouteGuard: Understanding and Mitigating Adversarial Risks for LLM Routing
comment: 15 pages, 13 figures
summary: Recent advancements in multi-model AI systems have leveraged LLM routers to reduce computational cost while maintaining response quality by assigning queries to the most appropriate model. However, as classifiers, LLM routers are vulnerable to novel adversarial attacks in the form of LLM rerouting, where adversaries prepend specially crafted triggers to user queries to manipulate routing decisions. Such attacks can lead to increased computational cost, degraded response quality, and even bypass safety guardrails, yet their security implications remain largely underexplored. In this work, we bridge this gap by systematizing LLM rerouting threats based on the adversary's objectives (i.e., cost escalation, quality hijacking, and safety bypass) and knowledge. Based on the threat taxonomy, we conduct a measurement study of real-world LLM routing systems against existing LLM rerouting attacks. The results reveal that existing routing systems are vulnerable to rerouting attacks, especially in the cost escalation scenario. We then characterize existing rerouting attacks using interpretability techniques, revealing that they exploit router decision boundaries through confounder gadgets that prepend queries to force misrouting. To mitigate these risks, we introduce RerouteGuard, a flexible and scalable guardrail framework for LLM rerouting. RerouteGuard filters adversarial rerouting prompts via dynamic embedding-based detection and adaptive thresholding. Extensive evaluations in three attack settings and four benchmarks demonstrate that RerouteGuard achieves over 99% detection accuracy against state-of-the-art rerouting attacks, while maintaining negligible impact on legitimate queries. The experimental results indicate that RerouteGuard offers a principled and practical solution for safeguarding multi-model AI systems against adversarial rerouting.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and systematizes LLM rerouting attacks that exploit LLM routers in multi-model systems, demonstrates their practical impact through a measurement study, and proposes RerouteGuard—a highly effective, scalable defense using dynamic embeddings and adaptive thresholds to detect and block adversarial rerouting with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: LLM routers in multi-model AI systems are vulnerable to adversarial 'LLM rerouting' attacks that manipulate routing decisions via crafted triggers, leading to increased costs, degraded quality, and safety bypass; these security risks are underexplored.
AI.method: The authors systematize LLM rerouting threats into a taxonomy based on adversary objectives and knowledge, conduct a measurement study on real-world systems, analyze attack mechanisms via interpretability techniques, and propose RerouteGuard—a dynamic embedding-based detection framework with adaptive thresholding to filter adversarial prompts.
AI.result: Real-world LLM routing systems are vulnerable to rerouting attacks, especially for cost escalation; RerouteGuard achieves over 99% detection accuracy across three attack settings and four benchmarks while preserving performance on legitimate queries.
AI.conclusion: RerouteGuard provides a principled and practical solution to defend multi-model AI systems against adversarial LLM rerouting attacks with high detection accuracy and minimal impact on legitimate queries.

title: Predicting Developer Acceptance of AI-Generated Code Suggestions
summary: AI-assisted programming tools are widely adopted, yet their practical utility is often undermined by undesired suggestions that interrupt developer workflows and cause frustration. While existing research has explored developer-AI interactions when programming qualitatively, a significant gap remains in quantitative analysis of developers' acceptance of AI-generated code suggestions, partly because the necessary fine-grained interaction data is often proprietary. To bridge this gap, this paper conducts an empirical study using 66,329 industrial developer-AI interactions from a large technology company. We analyze features that are significantly different between accepted code suggestions and rejected ones. We find that accepted suggestions are characterized by significantly higher historical acceptance counts and ratios for both developers and projects, longer generation intervals, shorter preceding code context in the project, and older IDE versions. Based on these findings, we introduce CSAP (Code Suggestion Acceptance Prediction) to predict whether a developer will accept the code suggestion before it is displayed. Our evaluation of CSAP shows that it achieves the accuracy of 0.973 and 0.922 on imbalanced and balanced dataset respectively. Compared to a large language model baseline and an in-production industrial filter, CSAP relatively improves the accuracy by 12.6\% and 69.5\% on imbalanced dataset, and improves the accuracy by 87.0\% and 140.1\% on balanced dataset. Our results demonstrate that targeted personalization is a powerful approach for filtering out code suggestions with predicted rejection and reduce developer interruption. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first quantitative study of code suggestion acceptance on large-scale industrial data, and this work also sheds light on an important research direction of AI-assisted programming.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a large-scale empirical study on AI code suggestion acceptance, identifying key behavioral and contextual features. It proposes CSAP, a high-accuracy model to predict whether developers will accept suggestions, enabling smarter, personalized filtering to reduce interruptions.
AI.motivation: Existing studies on AI-assisted programming are largely qualitative, and quantitative analysis of code suggestion acceptance is hindered by lack of access to fine-grained industrial interaction data. This work bridges the gap by analyzing large-scale proprietary data to understand and predict developer acceptance.
AI.method: Empirical analysis of 66,329 real-world developer-AI interactions from a large tech company to identify features distinguishing accepted vs. rejected code suggestions; development and evaluation of CSAP, a predictive model for code suggestion acceptance.
AI.result: Accepted suggestions are associated with higher historical acceptance rates (developer/project), longer generation intervals, shorter code context, and older IDE versions. CSAP achieves 0.973 (imbalanced) and 0.922 (balanced) accuracy, outperforming an LLM baseline and production filter by up to 69.5% and 140.1% respectively in accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Targeted personalization through CSAP is a powerful approach to filter out likely-rejected code suggestions, reduce developer interruptions, and improve the practical utility of AI-assisted programming tools.

title: On the Adversarial Robustness of Large Vision-Language Models under Visual Token Compression
comment: Under Review, 20 pages
summary: Visual token compression is widely used to accelerate large vision-language models (LVLMs) by pruning or merging visual tokens, yet its adversarial robustness remains unexplored. We show that existing encoder-based attacks can substantially overestimate the robustness of compressed LVLMs, due to an optimization-inference mismatch: perturbations are optimized on the full-token representation, while inference is performed through a token-compression bottleneck. To address this gap, we propose the Compression-AliGnEd attack (CAGE), which aligns perturbation optimization with compression inference without assuming access to the deployed compression mechanism or its token budget. CAGE combines (i) expected feature disruption, which concentrates distortion on tokens likely to survive across plausible budgets, and (ii) rank distortion alignment, which actively aligns token distortions with rank scores to promote the retention of highly distorted evidence. Across diverse representative plug-and-play compression mechanisms and datasets, our results show that CAGE consistently achieves lower robust accuracy than the baseline. This work highlights that robustness assessments ignoring compression can be overly optimistic, calling for compression-aware security evaluation and defenses for efficient LVLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CAGE, a compression-aware adversarial attack that exposes the overestimated robustness of compressed vision-language models by aligning perturbation optimization with actual compression inference, revealing the need for compression-aware security evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial attacks on large vision-language models (LVLMs) evaluate robustness using full visual token representations, ignoring the impact of token compression used during inference. This leads to an optimization-inference mismatch, resulting in overly optimistic robustness estimates for compressed models.
AI.method: The authors propose CAGE (Compression-AliGnEd attack), which aligns perturbation optimization with the compression process without requiring knowledge of the specific compression mechanism or token budget. It uses two components: (i) expected feature disruption to focus perturbations on tokens likely to be retained, and (ii) rank distortion alignment to ensure highly distorted tokens are preserved during compression.
AI.result: CAGE consistently achieves lower robust accuracy across various LVLMs, compression methods, and datasets compared to baseline attacks, demonstrating that traditional evaluation methods overestimate model robustness due to ignoring compression effects.
AI.conclusion: Ignoring visual token compression in robustness evaluation leads to misleading security assessments. CAGE reveals the true vulnerability of compressed LVLMs and underscores the necessity of compression-aware evaluation and defense strategies.

title: Adaptive Confidence Gating in Multi-Agent Collaboration for Efficient and Optimized Code Generation
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have catalyzed breakthroughs in automated code generation, Small Language Models (SLMs) often encounter reasoning bottlenecks and failure loops when addressing complex logical requirements. To overcome these challenges, we propose DebateCoder, a multi-agent collaborative framework designed to improve the reasoning ability of SLMs (e.g., Pangu-1B) in resource-constrained environments. DebateCoder uses a structured role-playing protocol with three agents: User Agent (A_UA), Technical Agent (A_TA), and Quality Assurance Agent (A_QA). It also includes an Adaptive Confidence Gating mechanism with a 95% threshold to balance accuracy and inference efficiency. In addition, we introduce a multi-turn deliberation module and a reviewer-guided analytical debugging loop for orthogonal pre-generation debate and post-generation refinement. Experiments on HumanEval and MBPP show that DebateCoder achieves 70.12% Pass@1 on HumanEval, outperforming MapCoder while reducing API overhead by about 35%. These results indicate that collaborative protocols can mitigate limitations of small-parameter models and provide a scalable, efficient approach to high-quality automated software engineering.

AI.tldr: DebateCoder is a multi-agent framework that enhances the reasoning capabilities of Small Language Models (SLMs) in code generation via structured debate, adaptive confidence gating, and iterative debugging, achieving strong performance on coding benchmarks with reduced API overhead.
